trial_name: PAMPer — Prehospital Plasma during Air Medical Transport in Trauma Patients at Risk for Hemorrhagic Shock (2018)
journal: The New England Journal of Medicine
citation: Sperry JL, Guyette FX, Brown JB, et al. Prehospital Plasma during Air Medical Transport in Trauma Patients at Risk for Hemorrhagic Shock. N Engl J Med. 2018;379(4):315-326
one_liner: Prehospital plasma during air medical transport for trauma patients at risk of hemorrhagic shock reduced 30-day mortality compared to standard resuscitation.

pico.population: Adult trauma patients (18–90 years) at risk for hemorrhagic shock (SBP ≤70 mmHg, or SBP 71–90 mmHg with HR ≥108 bpm) undergoing air medical transport.
pico.intervention: Prehospital transfusion of 2 units of plasma initiated during air medical transport, plus standard care.
pico.comparison: Standard prehospital resuscitation without plasma (crystalloids, red cells, or both).

background.existing_knowledge: Early trauma deaths are commonly driven by hemorrhage and trauma-induced coagulopathy with a narrow window for effective resuscitation. Observational data suggested potential benefit from earlier plasma.
background.knowledge_gap: In most civilian systems, plasma is initiated after hospital arrival due to logistical delays, pushing first plasma beyond the peak hemorrhage mortality window.
background.hypothesis: In trauma patients at risk for hemorrhagic shock transported by air, prehospital transfusion of 2 units of plasma reduces 30-day mortality compared with standard prehospital resuscitation without plasma.

methods.design: Multicentre, pragmatic, cluster-randomised, crossover trial with air medical base-level assignment alternating in 1-month blocks.
methods.setting: 27 air medical bases and 10 receiving trauma centres (9 Level I, 1 Level II) in the US from May 2014 to October 2017.

inclusion: Physiologic at-risk criteria: SBP ≤70 mmHg, or SBP 71–90 mmHg with HR ≥108 beats/min
exclusion: Burn injury >5% total body surface area

methods.intervention: Prehospital transfusion of 2 units of thawed plasma stored onboard and administered as early as feasible during air transport, in addition to standard resuscitation.
methods.comparison: Standard prehospital resuscitation without plasma, consisting of crystalloids, red cells, or both according to local protocols.
methods.blinding: Unblinded prehospital teams; primary endpoint (mortality) is objective.
methods.sample_size_power: 564 planned (cluster multiplier 1.75, 12% missingness) to provide 88% power to detect a 14% absolute mortality reduction (22% to 8%) at two-sided alpha 0.05 (adjusted to 0.037 for two interim analyses). Analyzed using GEE accounting for clustering.
secondary_outcomes: Total blood components transfused in first 24 hours
methods.follow_up: 30 days for primary endpoint; index admission (including first 24 hours) for in-hospital and early physiological/transfusion outcomes.

headline_bullets: Enrolled 523 patients across 27 bases; 501 comprised the modified intention-to-treat population (230 plasma, 271 standard care).
Prehospital plasma significantly reduced 30-day mortality from 32.8% to 23.0% (absolute reduction 9.8%, HR 0.64).
Survival curves separated early, accompanied by lower prothrombin-time ratio on arrival (1.2 vs 1.3; P<0.001).
Secondary mortality endpoints were concordant but lost statistical significance after multiple-comparison adjustment.

outcomes_table.note: Primary outcome data available for 220 vs 261; 10 outcomes imputed in each group
Adjusted P=0.55 after multiple comparison adjustment
Adjusted P=0.33 after multiple comparison adjustment

outcomes_table.outcome: Total blood components transfused in first 24h (median, IQR)
outcomes_table.note: Adjusted P=0.41 after multiple comparison adjustment
Adjusted P<0.001 after multiple comparison adjustment
Adjusted P>0.99 after multiple comparison adjustment

safety: Allergic or transfusion-related reactions occurred in 5/230 (2.2%) in the plasma group vs 1/271 (0.4%) in the standard care group (absolute difference 1.8%, 95% CI -0.2 to 3.8; P=0.10; adjusted P>0.99).

domains.notes: Cluster randomisation at air medical base with monthly crossover reduced stable centre confounding but permitted month-level drift and lacked allocation concealment.
Unblinded teams influenced co-interventions (fluids, red cells); primary mortality endpoint remains objective.
564 eligible, 523 enrolled, 501 analyzed in mITT (230 plasma, 271 standard care); primary outcome imputed in 20 patients (10 per group).
In plasma group, 205/230 (89.1%) received 2 units, 21/230 (9.1%) received 1 unit, and 4/230 (1.7%) received 0 units.

Injury Severity Score was similar (median ISS 22 in both groups). Co-intervention separation occurred: prehospital red cells (26.1% plasma vs 42.1% standard care; P<0.001) and prehospital crystalloid volume (median 700 mL vs 900 mL; P=0.03). Transport time was similar (40 vs 42 min).

internal_validity.verdict: Moderate internal validity due to unblinded co-intervention separation in crystalloids and red cells, offset by cluster crossover design and an objective primary endpoint.

domains.notes: Severely injured adult trauma patients with profound hypotension or hypotension plus tachycardia (median ISS 22).
Requires mature air medical cold-chain logistics and blood bank workflows with prehospital transport times averaging ~40 minutes; less applicable to short ground transport.

external_validity.verdict: Generalisable primarily to air medical transport systems caring for severely hypotensive trauma patients with prehospital times exceeding 20 minutes.

strengths: Pragmatic multicentre cluster-crossover design mitigating stable centre confounding
Clinically meaningful primary endpoint of 30-day mortality
High protocol adherence with 89.1% receiving full 2-unit dose
Mechanistic biological coherence demonstrated by improved prothrombin-time ratio on arrival
limitations: Unblinded design with measurable separation in co-interventions (lower red cell and crystalloid use in plasma group)
Post-screening exclusions and missing primary outcome data requiring imputation (n=20)
Secondary outcomes lost statistical support after multiple-comparison adjustments
High operational complexity and system dependency limit applicability in short-transport or low-resource settings

critical_appraisal.summary: Pragmatic cluster-crossover trial demonstrating a 30-day mortality reduction with prehospital plasma in air-transported hypotensive trauma patients, limited by unblinded co-intervention bias.
strengths: Cluster crossover design reducing institutional confounding
weaknesses: Unblinded administration causing co-intervention differences in red cells and crystalloids
Missing data requiring outcome imputation in 20 patients

sections.authors_conclusion: In trauma patients at risk for hemorrhagic shock, prehospital plasma transfusion during air medical transport resulted in significantly lower 30-day mortality than standard care.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: Prehospital plasma is effective for reducing 30-day mortality in severely hypotensive trauma patients undergoing air medical transport.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Adult trauma patients at risk of hemorrhagic shock (SBP ≤70 mmHg, or SBP 71–90 with HR ≥108 bpm) managed by air EMS systems with transport times >20 minutes.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: Does not imply benefit for short ground transport times, low-risk trauma without shock, or systems lacking blood bank cold-chain infrastructure.
implementation_caveats: Requires complex blood bank and air EMS cold-chain logistics for thawed plasma storage
Effect is partially confounded by lower prehospital crystalloid and RBC administration in the intervention group

controversies.notes: The COMBAT trial showed no mortality benefit for prehospital plasma during urban ground transport, raising concern that benefit is transport-time dependent.

Significant differences in prehospital red cell (26.1% vs 42.1%) and crystalloid administration (700 mL vs 900 mL), along with unmeasured adjunct therapies (TXA, cryoprecipitate), introduce residual confounding.
Pooled post-hoc analysis of PAMPer and COMBAT suggested survival benefit was concentrated when transport times exceeded 20 minutes.
RePHILL trial evaluating prehospital RBCs plus lyophilized plasma showed non-significant outcome differences, supporting context-dependent efficacy.
European trauma guidelines offer conditional recognition of prehospital blood products, reflecting persistent evidence heterogeneity.

context_related_trials.relation: Urban ground-transport RCT of prehospital plasma showing neutral mortality results, contrasting with PAMPer.
UK prehospital RCT evaluating RBCs plus lyophilized plasma which found no significant mortality benefit.

unresolved_questions: What is the precise transport-time threshold required to derive mortality benefit from prehospital plasma?
How does prehospital plasma interact with universal early prehospital tranexamic acid (TXA) administration?
Is prehospital plasma cost-effective when accounting for cold-chain logistics and blood product wastage?

quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: Prehospital plasma reduces 30-day mortality in air-transported trauma patients at risk of hemorrhagic shock, particularly when transport times exceed 20 minutes.
